title: Thamel, Patan or Boudha: where to stay in Kathmandu
meta_description: Where to stay in the Kathmandu Valley: Thamel, Lazimpat, Patan, Boudha or Bhaktapur compared for noise, access, price and character, with hotels we use.
summary: Stay in Thamel for convenience, nightlife and trek shopping; in Lazimpat or Durbar Marg for calm with central access; in Patan for Newar culture, cafes and quiet evenings; in Boudha to wake beside the great stupa. For a slower trip, add a night in Bhaktapur's old city or on the valley rim at Nagarkot or Dhulikhel.

sections.heading: The short answer
paras: Where you sleep shapes a Kathmandu trip more than most visitors expect. The valley's neighbourhoods are only a few kilometres apart, but traffic makes them feel further, and each has a different sound at night and a different walk in the morning. The best choice depends on what you came for.

For a first visit of two or three nights, especially before or after a trek, Thamel or nearby Lazimpat is easiest. For a culture-focused trip of four nights or more, Patan is our favourite base. For anyone drawn by Buddhism, or arriving late and leaving early, Boudha is close to the airport and wakes up to the sound of prayer wheels. Many of our journeys split the stay: a night or two in the city, a night inside an old town, a night on the rim.
Season matters too. In October, November and the spring festival weeks, the best small hotels in Patan, Bhaktapur and Boudha fill months ahead, so book early if you have a particular place in mind.

sections.heading: Thamel: convenient, lively, loud
paras: Thamel is the visitor district of Kathmandu, a grid of narrow lanes packed with guesthouses, trekking shops, bookshops, money changers, bars and restaurants serving everything from dal bhat to wood-fired pizza. It is about 6 km from the airport and a 20-minute walk from Kathmandu Durbar Square through the old market of Asan. Trekking agencies, permit offices and gear shops are all close, which is why trekkers love it.

The cost is noise and crowding. Motorbikes squeeze through lanes until late, bars play music into the night and touts are persistent. If you stay here, choose a hotel set back from the main lanes or with a garden. The Kathmandu Guest House, opened in the late 1960s and the area's best known address, has a quiet garden in the middle of the district. The streets to the south and west, towards Chhetrapati and Jyatha, are a little calmer, and the Garden of Dreams on the eastern edge is a peaceful escape.

sections.heading: Lazimpat and Durbar Marg: the quiet middle
paras: Just north and east of Thamel, Lazimpat and Durbar Marg are where embassies, older hotels and offices sit. You are a 10–20 minute walk from Thamel's restaurants but sleep in a calmer area, often in larger hotels with gardens and pools.

Hotel Shanker in Lazimpat occupies a white Rana-era palace with a garden. Hotel Yak & Yeti on Durbar Marg includes part of the old Lal Durbar palace and has long been one of the city's main five-star hotels. Durbar Marg runs up to the Narayanhiti Palace Museum, the former royal palace, and is lined with airline offices, banks and restaurants. This area suits families, older travellers and anyone who wants comfort and easy access without Thamel's late nights.

sections.heading: Patan: Newar culture and calm
paras: Patan, across the Bagmati River, is a separate city with its own Durbar Square, the finest museum in the valley and lanes full of Buddhist courtyards and metalworkers' workshops. Staying here means mornings in the square before the day visitors arrive and evenings when Newar families sit on temple steps and music groups practise.

Accommodation is mostly small: heritage guesthouses in restored brick houses near Durbar Square, boutique hotels and some larger hotels towards Jawalakhel and Kupondole. The Jhamsikhel and Sanepa areas, a short ride away, have many of Kathmandu's best cafes and restaurants and a large expatriate community. Patan is about 7 km from the airport. The trade-off is that Thamel's shops and trekking agencies are 30–40 minutes away by taxi, so trekkers who need to sort gear often start in Thamel and move to Patan afterwards.

Walk out of a Patan guesthouse at seven in the morning and you will see the city at work: women carrying offering plates to the Ganesh shrine on the corner, a priest washing the steps of a temple, men queuing for milk, the first hammer blows from a bronze workshop. That daily rhythm, more than any single monument, is the reason we suggest Patan to people who want to understand how the valley lives.

sections.heading: Boudha: the stupa at your door
paras: Boudha grew up around Boudhanath, one of the largest stupas in the world and the heart of Tibetan Buddhism in Nepal. Staying here means walking the kora at dawn with Tibetan grandmothers, eating thukpa and momo in Tibetan kitchens and hearing monastery horns at dusk. Evenings are quieter than in Thamel, and the area is only about 4 km from the airport, useful for early flights.

The Hyatt Regency Kathmandu sits in large gardens a short walk from the stupa, the most comfortable choice in the area. Around the stupa itself are many simple guesthouses, some run by monasteries, with rooftop views of the dome. Pashupatinath is about 3 km away. Restaurants are fewer and simpler than in Thamel or Patan, and most of the heritage squares are 30–45 minutes away by car.

Boudha is also the base for Kopan Monastery's courses on the hill to the north, for the thangka painting schools in the lanes around the stupa and for the big Tibetan festivals, Losar in February or March and Buddha Jayanti in spring, when the kora is packed from before dawn and every rooftop is strung with prayer flags.

sections.heading: Beyond the city: Bhaktapur, gardens and the rim
paras: Some of the most memorable nights in the valley are outside the main districts. Bhaktapur's old city has small guesthouses in restored houses; after dark the squares belong to residents, and early morning brings offerings and quiet lanes. It is about 14 km from the airport, convenient for departures.

Dwarika's Hotel, in Battisputali near Pashupatinath, is the valley's best-known heritage hotel, built around carved windows and doors saved from old Kathmandu houses. Gokarna Forest Resort sits inside a large old forest on the north-east edge of the valley, good for families and anyone who wants green space. On the rim, Club Himalaya at Nagarkot and Dwarika's Resort at Dhulikhel face the Himalaya, and a night at either gives you a sunrise over the mountains.

sections.heading: How to choose
paras: Ask yourself three questions. How long are you staying? For a night or two, pick convenience. What do you want to do most: trek shopping, temples, Buddhism or rest? And how do you feel about noise and crowds? Then consider splitting your stay. Two nights in Thamel or Lazimpat, two in Patan or Boudha and one on the rim is a pattern that works for many travellers, and the short transfers become part of the trip rather than a chore.

Whatever area you pick, a few things matter more than the star rating. Ask whether the hotel has a backup generator and filtered drinking water, whether rooms facing the street get traffic noise, and how far it is to a road a taxi can reach. In the old towns, some guesthouses are up steep wooden stairs, which matters if you have heavy bags or knee trouble. Our team checks these details for every place we use.

faqs.q: Is Thamel a good place to stay in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Thamel is the most convenient place for first-time visitors and trekkers, with hundreds of hotels, restaurants, gear shops and agencies, and a 20-minute walk to Kathmandu Durbar Square. It is also noisy and crowded until late. Choose a hotel with a garden or set back from the main lanes, or stay in quieter Lazimpat nearby.

For culture and calm, many travellers prefer Patan. It has its own Durbar Square, the Patan Museum, Newar food and a slower evening life, plus good cafes in nearby Jhamsikhel. Thamel is better for trek shopping, nightlife and the widest choice of budget rooms. If you have more than three nights, consider splitting your stay between the two.

faqs.q: Where should I stay in Kathmandu for an early flight?
faqs.a: Boudha is closest to Tribhuvan International Airport, about 15–20 minutes by car, and the Hyatt Regency or a guesthouse near the stupa works well. Dwarika's Hotel and Gokarna Forest Resort are also on the airport side of the city. Bhaktapur is about 45 minutes away. Thamel and Patan need 25–40 minutes, more at rush hour.

faqs.q: What is the best luxury hotel in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Dwarika's Hotel is the best known luxury heritage hotel, with courtyards of salvaged Newar woodwork and a Nepali restaurant serving long set meals. Hotel Yak & Yeti on Durbar Marg and the Hyatt Regency near Boudhanath are large five-star hotels with gardens and pools. Your choice depends on whether you want character, central access or space.

faqs.q: Is Boudha a good area to stay?
faqs.a: Yes, especially for travellers interested in Buddhism or meditation. You can walk the kora at dawn and dusk, visit monasteries and eat Tibetan food. Evenings are quieter than Thamel, and the airport is close. Fewer restaurants and a 30–45 minute drive to the Durbar squares are the main drawbacks.

faqs.q: Should I stay overnight in Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: If you have time, yes. Day visitors leave by late afternoon, and Bhaktapur's squares fill with residents, music and evening worship. Mornings are quiet and beautiful. Guesthouses in the old city are simple but comfortable and often in restored houses. One night is enough for most people; two allows a pottery class or a walk to Changu Narayan.

faqs.q: Is it safe to stay in Thamel?
faqs.a: Thamel is generally safe, including at night, with many people around until late. Normal precautions apply: watch for pickpockets in crowds, avoid empty lanes in the small hours and use registered taxis or ride apps. Touts selling tours or other goods are common but rarely aggressive; a polite no is enough.

faqs.q: Where do families stay in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Families often prefer quieter areas with gardens: Lazimpat and Durbar Marg hotels such as Hotel Shanker or Hotel Yak & Yeti, Gokarna Forest Resort on the forest edge, or Patan's family-friendly guesthouses. Avoid Thamel's busiest lanes with young children. A night at Nagarkot for sunrise is a family favourite.

faqs.q: How many nights should I spend in the Kathmandu Valley?
faqs.a: Three nights is the minimum to see the main heritage sites without rushing. Four to five nights lets you see all seven monument zones properly and add a night on the rim. Seven nights allows walks, a homestay and slower days in Patan and Bhaktapur. Add a night before any trek for gear, permits and rest.
